findings.title: Test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" does not actually verify denial cache precedence
findings.body: The sub-test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" in TestService_CacheCheck seeds the permission cache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} alongside an entry in permDenialCache. Because the permCache entry is already a denial for the requested resource, the test returns Allowed=false regardless of whether the denial cache branch is ever executed. If someone removed the permDenialCache check (or made the denial cache never match), the assertion would still pass because checkPermission would deny via permCache. To genuinely exercise denial-cache precedence over permCache, the permCache entry should be {dashboards:uid:dash1: true} (or another scope that grants the request) so that only the denial cache can explain the observed denial. As written, the test is a tautology that does not cover its claimed scenario, leaving the new code path untested.

findings.title: Denial cache key collides between anonymous and any identity with userUID "0"
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) is built solely from the parsed userUID. validateSubject parses "anonymous:0" to userUID "0" with identityType TypeAnonymous, but for any other identity whose UID is also "0" (e.g. a service-account or a user with numeric id 0 if such a record ever exists) the key namespace + ".perm_0_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent is identical. Consequently, an anonymous denial will incorrectly deny a same-UID user (and vice versa) for up to 30s. The key should include the identity type or use distinct prefixes per identity (e.g. anon.perm_..., user.perm_...) like permCache already does via anonymousPermCacheKey vs userPermCacheKey. The current naming userPermDenialCacheKey also misleads readers into thinking it only applies to real users.

findings.title: Permission-denial cache can mask newly granted access for up to 30s
findings.body: In Service.Check, when the DB lookup returns !allowed, the (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) tuple is written to permDenialCache with shortCacheTTL (30s). On any subsequent request for that exact tuple within the TTL, the denial cache short-circuits and returns Allowed=false without consulting permCache or the DB. This means workflows where a user gains access to a previously denied resource (e.g., an admin assigning a role that grants dashboards:read on a specific dashboard, or a service account being granted a folder) will be incorrectly denied for up to 30 seconds after the grant, despite the PR's stated goal of letting newly created dashboards/folders be accessible. Either the TTL needs to be much shorter, the denial cache must not be consulted before the permCache/DB for the freshly granted case, or some form of invalidation is required when permissions change.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage "false" label means "went to DB", not "cache unused"
findings.body: The new permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", action).Inc() call in Service.Check is reached both on a permCache miss (err != nil from getCachedIdentityPermissions) AND on a permCache hit that denies the request. In both cases we fall through to a getIdentityPermissions DB query. So the metric really tracks "did we have to query the DB", not "was the cache hit/missed". Combined with the symmetric requestCount.WithLabelValues(..., "true", ...) which is incremented on every code path after validateCheckRequest succeeds (cache hits, cache misses that went to DB, and errors during/after the DB call), the label "cached" is misleading. Either rename the labels (e.g., "served_from_db") or restrict "true" to genuine cache-hit responses so dashboards and alerts derived from these counters are meaningful.

findings.title: Existing "should deny user without permission" test does not verify the new denial cache population
findings.body: TestService_Check "User permission check" / "Anonymous permission check" already exercises the path that should populate permDenialCache (a Check that returns Allowed=false after going through getIdentityPermissions), but the assertions only check idCache and permCache, never permDenialCache. With the new code, a successful denial on the slow path must result in an entry under userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, userUID, action, name, parent); the test should assert that presence so that any future regression that drops the Set call is caught.

findings.title: "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" test does not verify the cache was refreshed
findings.body: The sub-test pre-seeds permCache with an outdated entry for dashboards:read (only dash1) and a DB that grants dash2, expecting Allowed=true via the fallback path. It does not assert that permCache was updated with the freshly fetched scopes including "dashboards:uid:dash2". Since the whole point of the fallback path is to keep permCache fresh, this should be asserted (e.g. require.Contains on s.permCache.Get for the new key).

findings.title: NoopCache methods have unused ctx parameter and unused receiver name
findings.body: The new NoopCache.Get/Set/Delete all declare ctx context.Context but never reference it, and the receiver is named lc (a leftover from LocalCache). Pass-though no-op types typically either omit the parameter (using the cache.Cache contract that doesn't require it) or use _ = ctx; the current shape will trigger unused-parameter linters and obscures the intent that these are pure no-ops. A short doc comment on the type explaining why this exists (in-proc client wants to skip the authlib local cache because the in-process server is already caching) would also help reviewers.
